question:
Rewrite this div-soup page using semantic HTML5 elements, and explain why it matters.
...
...
...
...
...
short:
**Replace generic `<div>` containers with semantic elements that expose accessibility landmarks and document structure to browsers, assistive tech, and search engines.**

- **Key mapping:** `<header>` (banner), `<nav>` (navigation), `<main>` (one per page), `<article>` (self-contained content), `<aside>` (tangential), `<footer>` (contentinfo).
- **`<article>` vs `<section>`:** use `<article>` for independently distributable content (a blog post, a card); use `<section>` for a thematic grouping with its own heading.
- **Accessibility gain:** screen-reader users can jump between landmarks directly instead of reading the whole page linearly.
answer:
Semantic elements convey **meaning and structure** rather than just being styling hooks. They matter for three concrete reasons:

- **Accessibility**: screen readers expose `header`, `nav`, `main`, `aside`, and `footer` as **landmarks**, letting users jump directly to regions. `<main>` should appear once and wraps the page's primary content.
- **SEO**: crawlers use the document outline (`article`, `section`, headings) to understand content hierarchy and importance.
- **Maintainability**: the markup self-documents intent without needing class names.

**Guidelines an interviewer looks for:**
- `<article>` = self-contained, independently distributable content (a blog post, a card).
- `<section>` = a thematic grouping, normally with its own heading.
- `<nav>` = major navigation blocks only, not every group of links.
- One `<main>` per page; do not nest it inside `article`/`aside`.

question: Build an accessible signup form: a name field, an email field, and a group of radio buttons for a contact preference. Show the correct way to associate labels and group related controls.
short:
**Every form control needs a programmatically associated `<label>`, and related controls (radios/checkboxes) need a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>` so assistive tech announces the group.**

- **Explicit association:** `<label for="id">` matched to the input's `id` — works even when not adjacent; placeholder text is not a substitute (it vanishes on input).
- **Grouping radios:** wrap them in `<fieldset>` + `<legend>`; screen readers announce the legend alongside each option so the user knows what question the radios answer.
- **Right `type` and `name`:** use `type="email"`, `required`, and give radios in a group the same `name` so only one can be selected.
answer:
Two things interviewers want to see:

1. **Every input has a programmatically associated label.** Use `<label for="id">` matching the input's `id`, or wrap the input inside the `<label>`. Placeholder text is **not** a label substitute — it disappears on input and is poorly announced.
2. **Related controls are grouped.** A set of radios or checkboxes that answer one question belongs in a `<fieldset>` with a `<legend>`. Screen readers announce the legend alongside each option, so the user knows the radios belong to "Preferred contact method".

**Other good practices:** use the right `type` (`email`), mark required fields with the `required` attribute (not just an asterisk), and give radios in a group the **same `name`** so only one can be selected.
code: Preferred contact method

question: Show how to use HTML5 input types and attributes to validate a form natively without JavaScript (email format, required, a number range, and a pattern).
short:
**Use semantic `type` values and validation attributes so the browser blocks invalid submissions and shows accessible error messages with no JavaScript.**

- **Useful types:** `email`, `url`, `number`, `date`, `tel` — each triggers the correct keyboard on mobile and enables automatic format checking.
- **Validation attributes:** `required`, `min`/`max`, `step`, `pattern` (+ `title` to describe the rule), and `minlength`/`maxlength` cover the most common cases.
- **Server validation is mandatory:** client-side constraint validation is a UX convenience only — always re-validate on the server.
answer:
HTML provides **constraint validation** that runs before submit, no JS required.

- `type="email"` / `type="url"` check basic format.
- `required` blocks empty submission.
- `type="number"` with `min`, `max`, and `step` constrains numeric range and granularity.
- `pattern="..."` applies a regex; pair it with `title` to describe the requirement in the error.
- `minlength` / `maxlength` constrain text length.

**Senior nuances:**
- Native validation is a **UX convenience, never a security boundary** — always re-validate on the server.
- Style validity states with the `:valid` / `:invalid` / `:user-invalid` pseudo-classes.
- You can override messages and styling via the Constraint Validation API (`setCustomValidity`, `checkValidity`).
- Use `novalidate` on the `<form>` if you want to handle validation entirely in JS.
code:
<form>
  <label for="em">Email</label>
  <input id="em" type="email" required>

  <label for="age">Age (18-120)</label>
  <input id="age" type="number" min="18" max="120" step="1" required>

  <label for="zip">ZIP (5 digits)</label>
  <input id="zip" type="text" pattern="[0-9]{5}"
         title="Enter exactly 5 digits" required>

  <button type="submit">Submit</button>
</form>

<style>
  input:invalid { border: 1px solid crimson; }
  input:valid   { border: 1px solid green; }
</style>

question: Given an informative product image, a decorative divider image, and an icon-only button, write the correct alt/labeling for each. Explain the rules.
short:
**Informative images get a descriptive `alt`; decorative images get empty `alt=""`; icon-only buttons need an `aria-label` because there is no visible text label.**

- **Informative `alt`:** describe what the image communicates in context, not what it depicts pixel by pixel; don't prefix with "image of".
- **Decorative `alt=""`:** empty but present tells screen readers to skip the image; omitting `alt` entirely is wrong and may cause the filename to be announced.
- **Icon buttons:** a bare `<button><svg>...</svg></button>` is announced as just "button" — always add `aria-label` or visually-hidden text.
answer:
`alt` text rules are a classic accessibility check:

- **Informative image** → concise `alt` describing the content/purpose (not "image of..."). Convey what the image communicates.
- **Decorative image** → `alt=""` (empty, but present). This tells screen readers to **skip** it. Omitting `alt` entirely is wrong — some readers then announce the file name.
- **Functional image** (image inside a link/button) → `alt` describes the *action/destination*, not the picture.
- **Icon-only button** → no visible text, so provide an accessible name via `aria-label` (or visually-hidden text). A bare `<button><svg>` is announced as just "button".

Rule of thumb: ask "if the image vanished, what text would I put here to preserve meaning?"

question: When should you reach for ARIA roles/attributes, and when should you NOT? Give an example of building an accessible custom toggle button, and explain the "no ARIA is better than bad ARIA" rule.
short:
**First rule of ARIA: don't use it if a native element already provides the semantics and behavior.**

- **Native `<button>` wins:** it is focusable, fires on Enter/Space, and announces its role for free — `<div role="button">` forces you to re-implement all of that.
- **When ARIA is appropriate:** use state attributes like `aria-pressed` or `aria-expanded` on a native control to express toggled/open states that have no native HTML equivalent.
- **"No ARIA is better than bad ARIA":** incorrect ARIA overrides real semantics and actively misleads assistive tech — wrong is worse than absent.
answer:
**First rule of ARIA: don't use ARIA if a native element does the job.** A `<button>` is focusable, keyboard-operable, and announced as a button for free. Slapping `role="button"` on a `<div>` forces you to re-implement focusability (`tabindex="0"`), Enter/Space handling, and disabled states — and getting any of it wrong leaves a broken control.

Use ARIA only to express **state and relationships native HTML can't**, for example:
- `aria-pressed` on a toggle button (on/off state)
- `aria-expanded` on a disclosure/menu trigger
- `aria-label` / `aria-labelledby` / `aria-describedby` for naming
- `aria-live` for dynamic announcements

**"No ARIA is better than bad ARIA":** incorrect ARIA *overrides* the element's real semantics, so a wrong `role` actively misleads assistive tech — worse than no ARIA at all. The example below keeps the native `<button>` and only adds the state attribute.

question: Explain tabindex values and fix this widget so a custom interactive element is keyboard-accessible. What is wrong with tabindex="5"?
short:
**`tabindex` controls whether an element is focusable and how it fits into the tab order; misuse breaks keyboard navigation.**

- **`tabindex="0"`:** adds the element to the natural tab order at its DOM position — use this for custom interactive elements.
- **`tabindex="-1"`:** focusable only via `el.focus()` in JavaScript, skipped by Tab — useful for programmatically moving focus.
- **Positive values are an anti-pattern:** `tabindex="5"` creates a separate tab sequence that runs before the natural order, making keyboard flow fragile and confusing — prefer native elements and DOM order instead.
answer:
**`tabindex` controls keyboard focusability and order:**
- `tabindex="0"` → element joins the **natural tab order** at its DOM position. Use this for custom interactive elements that aren't natively focusable.
- `tabindex="-1"` → element is **focusable programmatically** (`el.focus()`) but is **skipped by Tab**. Useful for moving focus to a region/heading after a route change.
- **Positive values** (`tabindex="5"`) are an anti-pattern: they create a separate, page-wide tab sequence that runs *before* the natural order, which is fragile and confusing. Avoid them.

A custom control also needs **keyboard event handling** (Enter/Space to activate) — focusability alone isn't enough. The real fix is usually to **use a native `<button>`** and skip all of this.
code: Go

question: Write the essential <head> metadata for an SEO- and social-share-friendly page: charset, viewport, title, description, canonical, and Open Graph tags. Explain what each does.
short:
**A well-crafted `<head>` covers rendering basics, search visibility, and social sharing through a layered set of meta tags.**

- **Rendering baseline:** `<meta charset="utf-8">` and `<meta name="viewport">` must be present on every page.
- **Search:** a unique `<title>` is the most important on-page SEO signal; `<meta name="description">` drives click-through from search results; `<link rel="canonical">` dedupes URLs.
- **Social sharing:** Open Graph `og:*` tags (title, description, image, url) control the preview card shown when the link is shared on social platforms and chat apps.
answer:
A strong `<head>` covers rendering, search, and social sharing:

- **`<meta charset="utf-8">`** — declare encoding; must be in the first 1024 bytes.
- **`<meta name="viewport">`** — required for responsive/mobile rendering.
- **`<title>`** — the single most important on-page SEO element and the browser-tab/label text; keep it unique per page.
- **`<meta name="description">`** — the snippet search engines may show; doesn't directly rank but drives click-through.
- **`<link rel="canonical">`** — tells crawlers the preferred URL when the same content is reachable at multiple URLs (avoids duplicate-content dilution).
- **Open Graph (`og:*`)** — controls the title/description/image of the **preview card** shown when the link is shared on social/chat apps. `twitter:card` covers X's variant.

Note `<meta name="keywords">` is **ignored by major search engines** — don't bother.
code:
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">

  <title>Best Trail Running Shoes (2026 Guide)</title>
  <meta name="description"
        content="Independent reviews of the top trail running shoes for 2026.">
  <link rel="canonical" href="https://example.com/trail-shoes">

  <!-- Open Graph (Facebook, LinkedIn, Slack, etc.) -->
  <meta property="og:type" content="article">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Best Trail Running Shoes (2026 Guide)">
  <meta property="og:description" content="Independent reviews for 2026.">
  <meta property="og:image" content="https://example.com/og/shoes.jpg">
  <meta property="og:url" content="https://example.com/trail-shoes">

  <!-- Twitter/X card -->
  <meta name="twitter:card" content="summary_large_image">
</head>

question: What does `<!DOCTYPE html>` do, and what happens if you omit it? Explain quirks mode vs standards mode with a concrete rendering difference.
short:
**`<!DOCTYPE html>` tells the browser to render in standards mode; omitting it triggers quirks mode, which emulates legacy IE bugs including a different box model.**

- **Standards mode:** triggered by `<!DOCTYPE html>`; the browser follows current CSS specs and uses `content-box` by default.
- **Quirks mode:** a missing/invalid doctype reverts to 1990s browser behavior — `width` historically included padding and border (border-box-like), so the same CSS produces different element sizes.
- **Check at runtime:** `document.compatMode` returns `"CSS1Compat"` for standards mode and `"BackCompat"` for quirks mode.
answer:
The doctype isn't an HTML tag — it's an instruction that tells the browser **which rendering mode** to use.

- `<!DOCTYPE html>` → **standards mode**: the browser follows modern W3C/WHATWG layout and CSS rules.
- Omitting it (or using an unknown/old doctype) → **quirks mode**: the browser emulates 1990s-era bugs for backward compatibility. There's also a rarely-relevant *almost-standards* mode.

**Concrete difference — the box model:** in quirks mode, an element's `width` historically *included* padding and border (the legacy IE box model). In standards mode the default is `content-box` (width = content only). So a `width: 200px; padding: 20px` box is **200px wide in quirks mode** but **240px wide in standards mode**. Other quirks affect line-height of inline images in table cells, percentage heights, and more.

Always start documents with `<!DOCTYPE html>`. You can check with `document.compatMode` (`"CSS1Compat"` = standards, `"BackCompat"` = quirks).
code:
<!DOCTYPE html>  <!-- must be the very first line: standards mode -->
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8">
    <title>Standards mode</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script>
      // "CSS1Compat" => standards mode, "BackCompat" => quirks mode
      console.log(document.compatMode);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

question: Serve responsive images two ways: (1) the same image at multiple resolutions with srcset/sizes, and (2) art direction / format fallback with <picture>. When do you use each?
short: **Use `srcset`+`sizes` when you want the browser to pick the best resolution of the same image; use ``+`` when you need a different crop or format per condition.** - **`srcset`+`sizes`:** provide width-descriptor candidates and rendered-width hints; the browser picks the smallest file that looks sharp for the viewport and DPR. - **``:** first matching `` wins — use `media` for art direction (different crop on mobile) and `type` for format negotiation (AVIF/WebP with JPEG fallback). - **`` is required inside ``:** it is the mandatory fallback and the element that carries the `alt` text.
answer: Two distinct responsive-image tools: **1. `srcset` + `sizes` (resolution switching).** You provide the *same* image at several widths with `w` descriptors; `sizes` tells the browser the image's rendered width at various breakpoints. The browser then picks the smallest file that still looks sharp for the device's DPR and layout — saving bandwidth on small/low-DPR screens. The `src` is the fallback for old browsers. **2. `` + `` (art direction & format negotiation).** Use this when you need a **different image per condition** — e.g. a wide crop on desktop and a tight square crop on mobile (`media` queries), or to offer **AVIF/WebP with a JPEG fallback** (`type`). The browser picks the first matching ``; the inner `` is mandatory and provides `alt` plus the ultimate fallback. Rule: same picture, different sizes → `srcset`. Genuinely different image or format → ``.

question: Show how to lazy-load below-the-fold images and an iframe, and embed a video with multiple sources and captions. What are the trade-offs of lazy loading the hero image?
short: **Add `loading="lazy"` to off-screen images and iframes to defer their fetch until near the viewport; never lazy-load the above-the-fold hero, as it directly hurts LCP.** - **`loading="lazy"`:** browser-native deferral for `` and `
answer:
**Native lazy loading:** `loading="lazy"` defers an image's or iframe's download until it's about to scroll into view, cutting initial page weight and requests. `loading="eager"` (the default) loads immediately.

**Key trade-off:** never lazy-load the **above-the-fold / hero image** — it's usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, and deferring it *hurts* LCP. For that image use `loading="eager"` and consider `fetchpriority="high"`. Lazy-loading is for content *below the fold*.

**Media:** `<video>` accepts multiple `<source>` elements so the browser picks a format it supports (WebM, then MP4 fallback). Add a `<track kind="captions">` for accessibility, set `controls`, and add `width`/`height` (or an aspect-ratio) to prevent layout shift. The text between the tags is fallback for browsers that can't play video.

question: Explain the difference between a plain <script>, <script async>, and <script defer>. Predict how each affects HTML parsing and execution order, and which you'd use for app code vs an independent analytics snippet.
short:
**A plain `<script>` blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and runs; `async` and `defer` both download in parallel but differ in when execution happens.**

- **`async`:** executes as soon as it arrives, pausing the parser at that moment; order between multiple async scripts is not guaranteed — best for independent analytics or ad tags.
- **`defer`:** execution waits until parsing finishes, then runs in document order just before `DOMContentLoaded` — best for app code that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts.
- **Modules:** `<script type="module">` is deferred by default.
answer:
All three only matter for **external** scripts (`src`).

- **Plain `<script src>`**: the parser **stops**, downloads the script, executes it, then resumes. Render-blocking — worst for performance if placed in `<head>`.
- **`async`**: downloaded **in parallel** with parsing; **executes as soon as it arrives**, pausing the parser at that moment. Order between multiple async scripts is **not guaranteed** (whoever downloads first runs first). Best for **independent** scripts with no dependencies — analytics, ads.
- **`defer`**: downloaded in parallel; **execution is deferred until parsing completes**, and deferred scripts run **in document order**, right before `DOMContentLoaded`. Best for **your app code** that touches the DOM or depends on other scripts.

**Rule of thumb:** `defer` for ordered app/module code; `async` for fire-and-forget third-party snippets. (Note: `type="module"` scripts are deferred by default.)
code:
<head>
  <!-- App code: needs DOM + ordered execution -->
  <script src="vendor.js" defer></script>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
  <!-- runs after parse, vendor.js before app.js -->

  <!-- Independent analytics: order irrelevant, run ASAP -->
  <script src="https://cdn.example.com/analytics.js" async></script>
</head>

<!-- Timeline summary:
  plain : parse | [stop + download + run] | parse
  async : parse --------+(run on arrival)+-------- parse
  defer : parse ----------------------------- | run in order | DOMContentLoaded
-->

question: What renders here, and why? Set the spans so the two boxes sit side by side AND respect width/height, without changing the markup. Explain block vs inline vs inline-block.
short:
**Block elements stack vertically and fill the available width; inline elements flow in text and ignore `width`/`height`; inline-block flows inline but honors box dimensions.** - **Block** (`
`, `

`):** starts on a new line, fills available width, respects all box-model properties. - **Inline** (``, ``):** sits alongside text, only as wide as its content — `width`/`height` and vertical margins are ignored. - **Inline-block:** the hybrid — flows inline but accepts `width`, `height`, and vertical padding/margin like a block; classic use for sized nav links or badges in a row.
answer:
**The three display models:**
- **block** (`div`, `p`, `section`): starts on a new line, takes the **full available width**, and respects `width`/`height`/all margins. Stacks vertically.
- **inline** (`span`, `a`, `em`): flows **within a line** alongside text, only as wide as its content. **Ignores `width`/`height`** and top/bottom margins (horizontal padding/margin work but don't affect line layout normally).
- **inline-block**: flows inline (sits **next to** other inline content) **but honors `width`, `height`, and all margins/padding** like a block. It's the classic way to lay out sized boxes on one line.

In the snippet, the spans are inline by default, so `width`/`height` are ignored and they only take content size. Setting `display: inline-block` makes them sit side by side *and* obey the dimensions. (Modern layouts often use fl/grid instead, but the distinction is core knowledge.)
code: A B

question: How do you store custom data on an element and read it from JavaScript and CSS? Write an example using data-* attributes and the dataset API.
short:
**`data-*` attributes store custom metadata on elements; JS reads/writes them via `element.dataset` with camelCased keys, and CSS can target them with attribute selectors.**

- **`dataset` API:** `data-user-id` becomes `el.dataset.userId` (kebab → camelCase); values are always strings — parse numbers or JSON yourself.
- **CSS attribute selectors:** `[data-state="open"]` lets you style state purely in CSS without extra classes.
- **Event delegation pattern:** attach one listener on the container and read `e.target.closest('[data-id]').dataset` — scales to dynamically added items.
answer:
`data-*` attributes are the standards-compliant way to attach **custom data** to elements without inventing non-standard attributes.

**Reading in JavaScript — the `dataset` API:** each `data-foo-bar` becomes `element.dataset.fooBar` (the hyphenated name is converted to camelCase). Values are always **strings**, so parse numbers/JSON yourself. Setting `dataset.fooBar = 'x'` writes back the attribute.

**Using in CSS:** target them with attribute selectors, e.g. `[data-state="open"]`, and you can even surface the value with `content: attr(data-label)`.

**Good uses:** holding an id/config for an event handler, state flags for CSS styling, hooks for test automation. **Don't** use them as a database or for large blobs, and remember they're exposed in the DOM (not for secrets).
code:
<button id="row"
        data-user-id="42"
        data-state="open"
        data-config='{"role":"admin"}'>
  Toggle
</button>

<script>
  const el = document.getElementById('row');

  // data-user-id -> dataset.userId (camelCase), always a string
  console.log(el.dataset.userId);            // "42"
  console.log(Number(el.dataset.userId));    // 42
  console.log(JSON.parse(el.dataset.config)); // { role: "admin" }

  // Write back -> sets data-state="closed"
  el.dataset.state = 'closed';
</script>

<style>
  [data-state="open"]   { background: #d4f7d4; }
  [data-state="closed"] { background: #f7d4d4; }
</style>

question: Embed untrusted third-party content in an <iframe> securely. Explain the sandbox attribute and how to grant only the permissions you need.
short:
**`sandbox` turns an `<iframe>` into a deny-by-default security boundary — all privileges are stripped and you opt back in only what's needed.**

- **Bare `sandbox`:** no scripts, no forms, no popups, and the frame is treated as a unique opaque origin with no access to the parent's cookies or storage.
- **Selective re-enable:** add only required tokens such as `allow-scripts` or `allow-forms`, following least-privilege.
- **Do not combine `allow-scripts` + `allow-same-origin`:** for untrusted content this pairing lets the frame remove its own sandbox.
answer:
The `sandbox` attribute turns an iframe into a **least-privilege boundary**: with a bare `sandbox`, the embedded page runs with **all restrictions on** — no scripts, no forms, no popups, treated as a **unique opaque origin** (so no access to your cookies/storage), no top-navigation, no plugins.

You then **re-grant only what's needed** via space-separated tokens:
- `allow-scripts` — run JS
- `allow-forms` — submit forms
- `allow-popups` — `window.open`/target=_blank
- `allow-same-origin` — keep its real origin (storage/cookies)
- `allow-popups-to-escape-sandbox`, `allow-top-navigation`, etc.

**Critical security note:** combining `allow-scripts` **and** `allow-same-origin` for untrusted content effectively lets the frame **remove its own sandbox** (it can rewrite its parent's `<iframe>` element if same-origin). For genuinely untrusted embeds, grant `allow-scripts` *or* `allow-same-origin`, not both. Also add `referrerpolicy` and a `title` for accessibility.
code:
<!-- Bare sandbox: maximum lockdown -->
<iframe src="https://untrusted.example.com/widget"
        sandbox
        title="Untrusted widget"></iframe>

<!-- Grant the minimum needed (scripts only) -->
<iframe src="https://untrusted.example.com/widget"
        sandbox="allow-scripts"
        referrerpolicy="no-referrer"
        title="Untrusted widget"></iframe>

<!-- DANGER for untrusted content: this pair lets the
     frame escape its own sandbox -->
<!-- sandbox="allow-scripts allow-same-origin" -->

question: Compare localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies. Write code that stores a value in each, and explain when to use which.
short:
**`localStorage` persists across sessions, `sessionStorage` clears on tab close, and cookies are sent on every HTTP request — choose based on who needs the data (client vs server) and how long it must last.**

- **localStorage:** persists until cleared (~5 MB); ideal for UI preferences and non-sensitive caches that should survive page reloads and restarts.
- **sessionStorage:** scoped to one tab/session (~5 MB); ideal for per-tab transient state like multi-step form drafts.
- **Cookies:** ~4 KB, automatically attached to every matching request; use for auth tokens the server must read; always set `HttpOnly`, `Secure`, and `SameSite` — never store secrets in Web Storage.
answer:
**Web Storage (localStorage / sessionStorage):**
- Key/value **strings only** (JSON-encode objects), ~5MB, synchronous, accessed via JS.
- **Never sent to the server** automatically — purely client-side.
- `localStorage` **persists** until explicitly cleared (survives restarts); `sessionStorage` is scoped to **one tab/session** and cleared when the tab closes.

**Cookies:**
- Tiny (~4KB), **automatically attached to every HTTP request** to the matching domain — which is the point: the **server** can read them. Also adds request overhead.
- Support `Expires`/`Max-Age`, and security flags: **`HttpOnly`** (hidden from JS, mitigates XSS theft), **`Secure`** (HTTPS only), **`SameSite`** (CSRF mitigation).

**When to use which:**
- Auth tokens / session IDs the server must read → **cookie** (ideally `HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite`).
- UI prefs, cached non-sensitive data that should persist → **localStorage**.
- Per-tab transient state (a multi-step form draft) → **sessionStorage**.

Never store secrets in localStorage — any XSS can read it.

question: When would you choose <canvas> over <svg> (and vice versa)? Draw a simple shape in each and explain the trade-offs around scalability, accessibility, and interactivity.
short:
**SVG is retained-mode vector DOM — scalable, styleable, individually accessible; Canvas is immediate-mode raster pixels — fast for large numbers of objects but not a DOM.**

- **SVG:** each shape is a DOM node with CSS styling, event listeners, and ARIA support; resolution-independent; performance degrades with very large element counts.
- **Canvas:** shapes are pixels drawn via JS API; the browser keeps no per-shape model — hit-testing, animation, and accessibility are all manual.
- **Rule:** few interactive scalable shapes → SVG; high-frequency rendering, games, or image processing → Canvas.
answer:
**SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics):**
- **Retained mode**: each shape is a **DOM node** you can style with CSS, attach event listeners to, and inspect.
- **Resolution-independent** — scales crisply to any size/DPI.
- **Accessible** — you can add `<title>`, `<desc>`, and ARIA; assistive tech can read it.
- Performance degrades with **very large numbers of elements** (each is a DOM node).
- Best for: icons, logos, charts, diagrams, anything that needs scaling or per-element interaction.

**Canvas:**
- **Immediate mode**: you draw **pixels** via a JS API; once drawn the browser keeps no object model. To "move" a shape you redraw the frame.
- **Raster** — blurs when scaled and is resolution-dependent.
- **Not accessible by default** (just a bitmap); you must supply fallback content/ARIA.
- Very fast for **thousands of objects**, pixel manipulation, games, and real-time visualizations.
- Hit-testing/interaction is manual (you track coordinates yourself).

**Rule:** few scalable, interactive, accessible shapes → SVG. Many objects / pixel work / animation-heavy → Canvas.
code:
<!-- SVG: vector, scalable, each shape is a DOM node -->
<svg width="100" height="100" role="img" aria-label="Blue circle">
  <title>Blue circle</title>
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="steelblue" />
</svg>

<!-- Canvas: raster, drawn imperatively via JS -->
